passage:
Note for Harsha's parents, Thursday
Today Harsha turned the reading corner into a ship bound for a moon made of idli. She gave every child a job: cook, captain, star-counter. At snack time she dipped her apple slice in her lemon rice "to see if it becomes a new fruit." She asked me why the moon doesn't fall. When one child called the ship game silly, her face dropped. I told the group that stories begin with ideas like hers, and we drew the ship a map. She brightened. Please keep asking her what she is building.
Usha, class teacher

qa.q: What did Harsha dip in her lemon rice?
qa.a: She dipped her apple slice in her lemon rice.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when another child called the ship game silly, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She seemed hurt, because her face dropped; she brightened again once Usha backed her idea.

qa.q: What choice did Usha make after the "silly" remark, and what did it change?
qa.a: Usha told the group that stories begin with ideas like Harsha's and drew a map with them, so the game went on instead of being shut down.

qa.q: What might the other children get out of Harsha's ship game?
qa.a: They each get a job and a story to step into, so the reading corner becomes an adventure for them too.

grounding: A child builds a make-believe world, asks why questions and tries odd food mixes, and needs an adult to protect her wondering from being called silly.

passage: In the courtyard behind the house, five-year-old Tushar crowned the calf king of the whole village with a marigold garland. "Why is the well water so cold? Why do crows hop? Why does the calf have no top teeth?" His sister Vidya, drawing water, laughed and answered what she could. When she suggested hopscotch again, like yesterday, Tushar groaned. "Same-same is boring." At lunch he stirred jaggery into his curd rice and called it royal food. Vidya almost said, "Don't be silly," and then stopped. "What does the king eat for sweet?" she asked. Tushar's eyes lit up.

qa.q: What did Tushar stir into his curd rice?
qa.a: He stirred jaggery into his curd rice.

qa.q: Why did Tushar groan at the idea of hopscotch?
qa.a: He felt bored at repeating yesterday's game and wanted something new, as "Same-same is boring" shows.

qa.q: What choice did Vidya make at lunch, and how did it help Tushar?
qa.a: She stopped herself from calling him silly and asked what the king eats for sweet, which let his make-believe keep growing.

qa.q: What might it be like for Vidya to have a brother who asks so many why questions?
qa.a: It can be a lot while she is busy drawing water, but she laughs, answers what she can and seems to enjoy joining his game.

grounding: A small child invents a pretend kingdom, asks many why questions and mixes foods, and his sister gives him room to wonder instead of calling him silly.

passage: On the balcony of their flat in Valencia, Valentina had turned the laundry basket into a rocket. 'Abuela Rosa, why does the moon follow our car? Is it lonely?' Before Rosa could answer, Valentina was mashing banana into her cheese sandwich. 'Moon people eat this.' Her cousin Pablo laughed. 'That's silly.' Valentina's face fell. Rosa sat down on the tiles beside the basket. 'Silly? I call it research. What else do moon people eat?' Valentina brightened and began to list: 'Cold rice. Jam soup. And stars, but only on Sundays.'

qa.q: What did Valentina mash into her cheese sandwich?
qa.a: Banana.

qa.q: How did Valentina feel when Pablo called it silly?
qa.a: She felt hurt and deflated; her face fell until Rosa took the moon game seriously.

qa.q: What did Abuela Rosa do that helped?
qa.a: She sat down, called it research, and asked a question inside the game, giving Valentina room to keep imagining.

qa.q: Why might Pablo see the sandwich so differently from Rosa?
qa.a: Pablo sees only an odd mix of food, while Rosa sees a whole make-believe world and chooses to join it.

grounding: Shows a young child building a make-believe moon world, asking why questions and trying odd food combinations, and needing room to wonder without being called silly.

passage: The colouring sheet was the same mango as yesterday and the day before. Yogesh coloured one corner, then slid under the table. 'It's a dinosaur hospital,' he told Tushar Sir, lining up three blocks as beds. 'Why didn't dinosaurs have doctors? Who fixed their teeth?' A girl nearby giggled. 'Dinosaurs are dead, silly.' Tushar Sir crouched down. 'Good question. Maybe other dinosaurs helped. Can you draw the hospital on the back of your mango?' Yogesh crawled out and filled the page with beds, a long-necked doctor and a bandage on a tail.

qa.q: What was on the colouring sheet?
qa.a: The same mango as yesterday and the day before.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh slide under the table after colouring one corner?
qa.a: He was bored by the repeated sheet and far more excited by the new world he was imagining, the dinosaur hospital.

qa.q: What did Tushar Sir's suggestion get right?
qa.a: He took the question seriously and linked the game back to the sheet, letting Yogesh's imagination do the work instead of forcing the same mango.

qa.q: What would change if Tushar Sir had agreed it was silly?
qa.a: Yogesh might have felt foolish and stopped asking, and the page of hospital beds would never have been drawn.

grounding: Shows a young child bored by repetition who builds a make-believe dinosaur hospital and asks why questions, and a teacher who gives room to wonder.

passage:
Monday. Sarita drew a snake across the hopscotch squares. 'If you land on its head, you slide back to one!' Her mother Madhuri, hanging out clothes, said, 'Just play it properly, don't be silly.' Sarita rubbed the snake out with her foot.
Wednesday. Sarita pushed the same carrom coins around, sighing, and asked no questions all evening.
Saturday. Madhuri picked up the chalk. 'Show me the snake game.' Sarita's eyes lit up. She added a ladder, then a river. 'Why can't snakes climb ladders, Amma?' 'You tell me,' said Madhuri, and hopped.

qa.q: What did Sarita draw across the hopscotch squares?
qa.a: A snake.

qa.q: Why did Sarita ask no questions on Wednesday?
qa.a: After being called silly she felt deflated and bored, so her usual wondering had gone quiet.

qa.q: What changed on Saturday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Madhuri joined the snake game and let Sarita make the rules, which gave her room to invent and wonder again.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see Monday differently by Saturday?
qa.a: Madhuri may have noticed how flat and quiet Sarita became, and seen that the 'silly' game was what made her lively.

grounding: Shows a child whose invented games and why questions fade after being called silly and return when a parent makes room for them.

passage: The power went out on the hottest night of May, and the flat went dark. Avni, five, gasped. "Papa, we're in a cave! There are bats!" She hung a dupatta from the chair and crawled under it. "Why do bats sleep upside down? Do they get dizzy? Do bats eat roti?" Uday, her father, sweating by the torch, didn't say "Don't be silly." He handed her a roti and a banana. Avni rolled them together. "Cave pizza!" She fed a pretend bat first. When the fan whirred back to life, she groaned. "Can we keep the cave?"

qa.q: What did Avni roll together?
qa.a: A roti and a banana, calling it cave pizza.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when the power went out?
qa.a: She felt excited and delighted, turning the dark flat into a cave full of bats.

qa.q: What did Uday do that gave Avni room to wonder?
qa.a: He didn't call her silly, answered her game by handing her food and let the make-believe continue despite the heat.

qa.q: How might Uday feel watching Avni feed a pretend bat?
qa.a: He may feel amused and fond of her imagination, even while hot and tired in the power cut.

grounding: Shows a child building a make-believe world, asking why questions and trying odd food combinations, excited by novelty and given room to wonder.
